utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, it would assist the Trial Chamber if you were to briefly outline where we are now and what you suggest ought to happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. First of all, I would address the issue of General Clark. In light of Appeals Chamber decision, Your Honour, we have decided or sort of reached the end of our road with General Clark, in terms of our Prosecution case in chief. We -- so we will no longer be attempting to add him to our witness list at this point, but that leaves us with the matter of Zoran Lilic, Your Honour. Mr. Stamp is here to address the Court about the situation with him and our request concerning trying to have him testify in our case in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please you, Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution on the 10th of April filed a notice indicating what the situation then was in respect of Mr. Zoran Lilic; and in that notice, we indicated that should the appeal in respect to General Clark be dismissed, we would move the Court to allow us to bring the witness to testify today, the 25th. Subsequent to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think that would be tomorrow, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, tomorrow would be the 25th. Yesterday, we filed a response to the Defence application, that we should be ordered to close the case and the Court would not have the benefit of hearing Mr. Lilic. And in that response, we set out the present facts and circumstances in respect of Mr. Lilic. He has been served with a subpoena by the district court. He has indicated he's willing to attend. However, for his personal health reasons, he would not be able to attend this week but for the week beginning the 1st of May, and that is the application. The facts supporting the application are set out in the filing of the 10th of April and the filing of yesterday evening. It clearly is a matter of the exercise of a discretion, which is within the jurisdiction of this Court. The Prosecution has shown, it is submitted respectfully, due diligence in trying to get him here. There is, of course, the issue of prejudice to the Defence, and the Court is, it is respectfully submitted, quite capable of balancing the interests of justice in hearing such an important and unique witness - that is what I'd like to stress; a unique witness - in circumstances where the inconvenience of the Defence would be just a matter of a couple of days. The 1st of May is just three court days away from today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: With the papers, there is an official note.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's confidential, but my reference to it won't, I think, raise any issue of breaching confidentiality. It says that he will be able to respond to the summons on the 29th of this month or the 6th of May; whereas, your submission doesn't refer to the 6th of May. What is the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The Victim Witnesses Unit and the relevant officers of the Tribunal have started proceedings to get him here on the 29th of May -- 29th of April, which I think is a Saturday or a Sunday. Therefore, he would be available to come to court on the 1st of May. We proceeded on that basis because we wanted to get him here at the earliest opportunity that he indicated his health would afford or enable him to travel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And there is reference to other conditions relating to attendance as well as an indication of a need for company. There appear to be a number of complications yet to be a addressed, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are in the process of addressing all of them. Those persons who will accompany him or who he has asked to accompany him, we will do what is necessary and appropriate in that regard. He has testified here before; and when he did attend here to testify in the past, there were persons who accompanied him and who were present in court, and I think - I think, I'm not sure - had the right of audience while he was present in court a representative of the government of the FRY at the time and also his own personal legal representative. We have not been able to speak with him, and we don't know what is the nature of the additional person. One person is his doctor. We don't know the nature of the additional person who is to accompany him. When we do discover that, we will, if necessary, make an appropriate application or at least a notification of that to the Court. However, as far as the transportation is concerned, my understanding is that we are taking all necessary and reasonable steps to have both Mr. Lilic and his medical doctor and other representative here for that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it you accept that there are a number of factors raised in this official note which formed no part of the previous report regarding the witness, which was filed on the 10th of April; and that in that report, a quite different reason was given for his non-attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the one he said would be here this week but, the reason he couldn't be here until this week is a quite different reason from the one that's now being given of the various reasons that are now being given for his non-attendance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The reasons are different, and we have not been able to inquire of him as to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: For example, one of them - and this isn't confidential - relates to a visa. Now, you arrange visas for people. That's not a problem for his attendance, surely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: We are settling that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He seems to be latching on to it, and it's clearly an irrelevant issue for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The declaration reproduces what he said, and I don't know his state of knowledge. As I said, we have not had an opportunity to interview him; and perhaps if we do, these concerns that he has raised might be explained. But the two main reasons that were given relating to medical health of himself and another person, without going into any further details, are different but not, it is submitted, necessarily inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp, the separate basis for opposing your motion relates to an alleged failure to disclose material. And in paragraph 7 of the Defence submission, it is said that the Prosecution was in possession of this material and that it was in the actual knowledge of the Prosecution for a considerable period. And it is suggested that there are over 4.000 pages of new material; and in your response, I think you say that you concede the lesser amount, but I think is it 800, over 800 pages?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're pointing to the fact that the pages which need to be reviewed by the Defence amount to 859, which are identified in your schedule. Is it your submission that you have not had this material for the length of time that the Defence suggest?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not sure if the Defence suggested a length of time. They said a considerable period. I'm not sure when the material was received. What I do know is that most of this material came up in a search that was done in April, the vast majority of these materials. These are newspaper reports that were obtained from various archives, I think, belonging to institutions or NGOs that over a period of time handed them into the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the particular nature of the search in April that would reveal material which may have been there before but hadn't been revealed to you in some way?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: To go into the operations of the evidence unit, of which I am not completely conversant with, I know that most of what we call open source material; for example, newspaper reports that we get from various organisation that collect them, for example, organisation that collect the newspaper reports from the former Yugoslavia, the Balkans, were not put in the system electronically until recently. Therefore, they would not come up in searches -- in all searches. What has happened - and this is something I should point out as well - is that with the advent of the electronic disclosure system, this material which was here unstamped, that is without ERN numbers, and not it scanned into the system was then scanned into the system to be made available to the Defence if they wanted to do their research or their searches for these material on EDS. The up shot of what I'm saying - without going into an area that I'm not completely familiar with - is that in many cases, open source material, newspaper reports, were scanned into the system just, recently and I can't how recently, but they would not come up in the earlier electronic searches in the system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you take as a particular example, it's said here that there are seven CDs of raw video interview of Mr. Lilic which were not disclosed before, is that accurate, that this was not disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I think, and I could check this and give a very accurate answer, but I believe these CDs were received very recently. I believe the BBC interviewed Mr. Lilic, and extracts from the interview were part of a BBC programme in respect of former Yugoslavia and that was disclosed. An effort was made recently to obtain the raw footage, and the raw footage was obtained and disclosed. And that is something I'd like to confirm, but I believe the raw footage was not something that has been in our possession for a considerable period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have the Defence submission and the schedule attached to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. But before we proceed, may I just confirm that with respect to the raw footage, we came into possession of it on the 17th of April this year. In other words, we had the BBC programme in which there were extracts of the interview. We thought it would be helpful to give to the Defence or find the entire interview and give it to the Defence, which is what we did. Sometimes in being overly helpful, it can result in inconvenience, I suppose is a more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When did you have that idea?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The idea?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Of getting the raw footage? How long has it taken you to get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I don't know how long it took to get it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's difficult to justify postponing a trial because all of a sudden you had an idea to go and look for more material and you got it back, and you thought it might help the Defence and you send it to them, especially when they don't want it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not commenting on their position whether as to whether they wanted it or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would help us to know how long, for example, you'd been trying to get this material. Was it just a thought in March, or was it something that had been ongoing for sometime?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Again, I can check to confirm what I'm about to say. I believe it was originally requested sometime ago during the Milosevic trial. Efforts were made to get it. There was a waning to some degree in terms of trying to get it, in way of efforts in trying to get it. But it has been something that we have been trying to obtain for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you look at page 5 of the schedule, which the Defence have provided, identifying what has been disclosed, you'll see right in the middle of page 5, I have has already disclosed some time ago interview, unedited, of Zoran Lilic. Now, is that the same interview in some other form than the CD recordings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. These -- the material identified in the middle as interview, unedited of Zoran Lilic by the Brook Lapping TV Production Company, these are the transcripts of the extracts of the entire interview that was conducted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They are transcripts of the extracts, the shorts, that's the parts that were broadcast in the documentary?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why the word "unedited"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I am not entirely sure why the word "unedited" is inserted here. I can -- well, let me not guess. I should advise the Court to be absolutely correct that we requested and obtained the transcript, the unedited transcript, during the Milosevic case. And the raw material, the video itself, we requested and obtained that recently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Having said that, though, Mr. Stamp, the number of pages involved is only 42, I think, which is difficult --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is why I indicated that I could not explain why it says unedited. That does indicate that it was edited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what are you telling me? That you disclosed the full transcript, unedited, of all the interviews at an earlier stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. All right. And did you have a full transcript of all?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is not known.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you go also to page 1 of this schedule? And there are two items -- in fact, there are three. Let me change that. There are four I want to ask you about specifically. The second blacked out section, "Letter dated the 30th April from Lilic to Milosevic"; and then the next blackout section, "Letter by Lilic to Milosevic dated the 30th of April," which I presume is a different letter. It certainly has different numbers, although the same date; and then the next section, "Letter dated 5th May 1999 by Lilic to Milosevic," and the third line of that section, "Unsigned ICTY witness statement of Zoran Lilic dated the 4th of December 2001." Now, have these four documents -- you tell me how long have these four documents been in the possession of the ICTY OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, I must confess that I could not say precisely. I could look at the ERN numbers and conclude that they have been in our possession for a matter of years. Your Honour, I would like to make further checks as to whether or not these documents were in fact not disclosed to the Defence at some earlier period. The Defence has represented that they were not, and I do not object to that. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You must agree with that if you have gone about disclosing them at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Many times, Your Honour, when documents and material are disclosed, even though when checks are made, it is discovered that they had been disclosed before. Documents of this nature, I can indicate, are likely to have been disclosed before, and I think -- I think it is almost a certainty -- well, again, I can confirm that the statement would have been disclosed, perhaps in another format with another number. When these searches are done, sometimes a document comes up and it is stamped with another number, and they are redisclosed. It happens sometimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I take it, though, that these were disclosed because you believed they hadn't been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: They were disclosed at the time, it is my understanding, because it was not confirmed that they had been in the past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: However, you're saying that the ERN numbers attributed to these would suggest that you've had them a long time. Would that not also suggest that they would be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: It would indicate to me. That is why documents of this nature --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why on earth would you disclose them now, unless you had a real reason to think they hadn't been?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The decision to disclose them, as I indicated, Your Honour, would have been made because at the time in the process of the disclosure, there was no confirmation that they had been disclosed. And in those circumstances, the decision is normally taken to disclose, to ensure that the material goes out to the Defence, even it is possible that the Defence might have had them before. As I said, I cannot confirm the Defence had them before, but I could check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there anything else you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I indicated, Your Honour has referred to some documents which are important or appear to be important on the face of them. I do know, in respect of unsigned statement, that at least one unsigned statement, which was substantially the same as this unsigned statement, was disclosed to the Defence a long time ago. And in respect to the other matters that have been disclosed recently, they are almost entirely open source material, newspaper reports, without minimising what the Defence has to do, that it is submitted would not prejudice the Defence in a manner that should preclude this witness from testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you been properly recorded in the transcript as saying, in respect of the unsigned statement, that at least one unsigned statement which was substantially the same as this unsigned was disclosed to the Defence a long time ago?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that one made at a different time?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In the procedure to get a statement from the witness, an unsigned statement was entered into the system with a number, and an attempt was made to have the witness sign it. He did not. A later attempt was made to have the witness sign substantially the same statement with a different number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But what does "substantially the same" mean? You mean exactly the same or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not exactly the same, I don't think. At least the number would have been different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis would it have been changed, for example?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: My understanding is that in all material particulars, practically the witness statement is the same. There might have been an additional person on the cover page for the interview. But in terms of the material, the substance of the statement, they are the same. A second attempt was made to have the statement signed; and when that attempt was made, the statement had been registered into the system with a different number. That had been served on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Finally, there is one document which is only available in Albanian. When did you get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is -- that is a document that I'll confirm shortly about how long ago we had that document. However, that is a document which the issue as to what part of it is relevant is a matter that could be, I respectfully submit, addressed with the Defence. Although the book has been disclosed, the notice indicates that there is only one page in which there is any reference, but I think the page number is not correct on this. But I don't think the issue here is an entire book. The book, when it is scanned, the reference to something relevant to the case might have been picked up, and I believe we can address that to the Defence by telling them precisely where in the book. I don't think the Defence -- and issues like this, I think, can be dealt with amicably between the parties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It was also published in April 1998 and that may be one reason why it's not terribly important, but can you answer the question when did you get it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In June 2001. The material like books, open source material, publications, various publications, documentaries, et cetera, come into the system by various means. They cannot be, because of the sheer bulk of them, be analysed individually. It is just impossible to have that manpower to do so. They have to -- we have to search for them electronically and find means and methods of trying to have what results from the search analysed by personnel that we have. The system of doing electronic searches for certain key words in archives with millions of pages of documents improves over time. Searches that are sometimes done three or four years ago or two years ago will pick up material using key words, but searches that are done now two years later will sometimes pick up additional material because the systems that are used have improved. However, it is impossible for us to try to find these materials by any other means but electronic searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This was a search, according to your own submission, carried out after the stage at which you anticipated closing your case in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: For this particular document, I do not know exactly when the search -- which search picked it up. I believe it might well have been searched in April. However, the searches are done from time to time. If for some reason the Prosecution's case did not close next week, and we continued in June, we would do a search in June; and if there is a substantial improvement in the technology, then it is possible that something might be found electronically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Surely, all of these documents now disclosed, which were disclosed on was it the 17th of April? Surely, they all emerged from the most recent search.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I believe most of them did. I could not say that they all did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So how could you have exculpatory material at an earlier date and not disclose it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As I say, I believe most of them did. There is -- when we are speaking about so many documents, this is not the only disclosure to the Defence. I think the Defence will tell that the disclosure to them has been enormous, gargantuan in a case like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In relation to Lilic. We are only concerned with Lilic at the moment, bear that in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But in respect of Rule 68, for a witness of this nature, there is always the possibility - and that is why I answered the question in that way - that some document might have come up in the system and for whatever reason, error or oversight, might not have been disclosed. So I believe that most if not all, I cannot say all, came up, I cannot responsibly say that it is impossible that something from the past, when we are dealing with so many searches and so much documentation, might not have come up before and not been disclosed. Part of the problem of disclosure here is that we are dealing with a combination of doing reasonable electronic searches and then having to analyse or to some degree review the results of those searches with scarce personnel. And in those circumstances, I could only say that we do the best that can be done, having regard to the present state of technology available to us and personnel available to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stamp. Mr. O'Sullivan, who will address this issue for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll take the lead on that, Your Honour. So far the questions from the Bench and the submissions by the Prosecution have dealt only with Rule 68.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Our submission goes beyond Rule 68, in asking you to declare this case closed, but let me first address the Rule 68 matters. We disagree that the electronic disclosure system alleviates any responsibility of the Prosecution to not fulfil its obligations under Rule 68. There seems to be, we say, some misunderstanding on the part of the Prosecution in relation to Rule 68. The Blaskic Appeals Chamber judgement, and also the Krstic Appeals Chamber judgments, make it clear that the duty on the Prosecution to disclose under Rule 68 is it is equal to its duty to prosecute. The Prosecution is obliged to disclose any and all material coming under Rule 68, even if there exists other information of a general similar nature. We used our best efforts over the weekend to determine which material had not been previously disclosed to us. That's in our annex. We disagree that the 859 pages identified by the Prosecution is sufficient for us to deal with the over 4.000 pages that are new to us. Now, it may be the Prosecution's view that there is only 859 pages. We certainly would have an obligation under any measure of due diligence to examine all those documents in their entirety, and perhaps focus on the pages the Prosecution has identified under its review of those documents. So we say that the Rule 68 has not been complied with in a timely fashion. It's been incomplete. Yesterday, we received the 7 CDs, and we still have the one document in Albanian. And might I add that Rule 68, of course, includes information that may go to the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or the credibility of a witness. So we say that those -- all those factors are matters that we have to examine in preparation for the testimony of a witness. But I said that our application requesting to you declare the case closed and to proceed with 98 bis in fact is threefold: First, and foremost, we ask you to enforce your order of the 23rd of March which was clear. It was unambiguous that in if the paragraph 9(C), if the Clark Appeal failed, then the Prosecution must call Mr. Byrnes and Mr. Lilic on the week of the 16th of April. Mr. Byrnes testified and Mr. Lilic was not available. But on top of that, given what happened on the 19th of April, with the disclosure, we say the lack of disclosure, incomplete disclosure, that we are not in the position to proceed and, therefore, you should exercise your discretion and close the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: At the 23rd of March, if I -- or certainly if it wasn't the 23rd of March, a day or two days beforehand, the Prosecution position was to rest their case and take a chance on being able to justify leading the evidence of Lilic on some other basis that one might try to do that after the closure of the case; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe that submission was made in respect to Clark, not Lilic or Byrnes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It couldn't have been made in relation to Clark.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Correct. The position, as I remember it, was that there would be a pending appeal; and if the appeal was successful, then they would reapply to bring Clark. They had abandoned Lilic and Byrnes. Let me turn to 65 ter. Our position there is that this Chamber had ordered, at the pre-trial stage, an annex C to the pre-trial brief, which would cross-reference every exhibit the Prosecution wished to tender, would cross-reference those exhibits to a witness. We've identified, in our filing, all the exhibits that are not cross-referenced to Mr. Lilic. The Chamber clearly ordered that in order to provide us the opportunity to prepare for trial, to investigate and prepare a cross-examination for every witness, including Mr. Lilic. We say that that order is based on our right to confront each witness, which is guaranteed by Article 21(4)(e) of the Statute, which provides that we have a right to confront, a right to examine each witness. Now, the Prosecution says, in their response, that under Rule 92 ter, all exhibits from the Milosevic trial would be part of the 92 ter package. Well, our response to that again is to look at the pre-trial brief. The pre-trial brief announced Mr. Lilic as a live witness who would testify for 12 hours. There is no basis to say that the Milosevic exhibits were a part or to be a part of his testimony. He was only announced as 92 ter last Thursday. So, again, since the pre-trial brief in 2006, we have been operating on the assumption he would be live and accede to the pre-trial brief announced which exhibits would be used, and the Prosecution cannot be heard to say that we were put on notice prior to the 19th of April, last week. So those are the three bases for our request to have you close the Prosecution's case; your order of the 23rd of March, and non-compliance with 65 ter and Rule 98. We've set out the prejudice in our -- Rule 68, excuse me. In our motion, we set out the prejudice that we say we incur if this trial is not closed. And might I add, we must say quite frankly to the Trial Chamber that, so far, this has been a high-paced intensive case and well-managed. For the last month, quite frankly, we have been floundering. And we are asking the Trial Chamber to retake control of the proceedings, declare the case closed, and guarantee and ensure to us a fair and expeditious trial. We say the Prosecution should not control proceedings, nor should a witness. And the prejudice and the detriment of the accused far outweighs any interests which the Prosecution has. They call Mr. Lilic an important and unique witness. At any time since last July, they could have called him. They abandoned him. The prejudice, as we've reiterated many times, to you in the last month, is that we are not having an opportunity to prepare our case, our Defence cases. We cannot intensely prepare as we've undertaken to do. We have lost a month. The Trial Chamber had given us two and a half months to file our 65 ter submission. I think there is a reason for that. You wanted us to work diligently, intensively, and only on our Defence cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That decision though was taken in light of the fact that there was a certified appeal to be disposed of, and that has at least yielded some bonus.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: At the same time that we are not working on our Defence cases entirely, or the way we would like to, we are also juggling two other balls. We are anticipating potential future witnesses, and we are also trying to work on the 98 bis submissions, which is no small feat given that they are completely oral. These issues, we want to presents coherent 98 bis submissions and complete 98 bis submissions. And Your Honour can appreciate that without the support of a written brief, we are having to revisit this on a regular basis; because when you take off the 98 bis hat and you start thinking about potential witnesses and dealing with investigators in your Defence case, every five or six or 10 days, you're going back to attempt to coherently prepare oral submissions, lengthy ones that are meaningful to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You at least must have yours prepared because you could be making them in half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, we ask you to do the right thing, and we say you should close the case and proceed to 98 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There is no technical issue here over who has to close the case?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, the Prosecution should be ordered to close the case pursuant to your March 23rd order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The Chamber will retire to consider this. --- Break taken at 11.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose I should apologise, first of all, for being early. The Chamber doesn't find this an easy decision to take. We have decided by majority to grant the Prosecution motion, which is to be allowed to call the witness Zoran Lilic on the 1st of May. In doing so, we have also decided to refuse to apply any sanctions against the Prosecution in relation to the Defence submissions about delayed or failure, it's really delayed, disclosure. The Prosecution raised -- sorry. The Defence raised another issue, which was the link between the witness and the exhibits, and related that to the question of the format of the witness's evidence; in other words, whether it was entirely live evidence or partially in writing, in terms of Rule 92 ter. Mr. O'Sullivan, now that we've decided to grant the motion allowing the witness to give evidence, would you like to make any further submission about whether that evidence should be entirely live or not? And if you want time to think about that, obviously, you can be given time. It's also one of these decisions that should probably be provisional. It would be helpful to have a decision in principle, but no doubt along the way that decision might change depending on the nature of what it might be the Prosecution try to tender; in other words, an extract from the transcript, for example, rather than what they are tendering at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had prepared for this witness on the assumption that he would testify live, and we think that's the way it should proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May it please, Mr. President, right throughout this case we have had situations where persons originally proposed as live witnesses have, for the sake of convenience and with a view of putting in effect the intendment of the revised -- or the new Rule 92 ter to shorten the proceedings and to make more effective the presentation, and naturally, of course, the witness has testified before on essentially the same substance and has done so over a matter of days. It may well be the most convenient and just approach, especially in regard to court time, that he proceed in the way envisioned by the Rule as it is now, as it has been changed. I would indicate that the 92 ter document that the Prosecution proposes to tender is redacted, because it is a significant amount of evidence he is able to give and it is redacted of material related to the pre-indictment period or to other areas of the territory of the former Yugoslavia. So I respectfully urge upon the Court that the Prosecution be allowed to put the evidence in pursuant to the provisions of Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm sorry. There was one additional factor I was just reminded of. This is a witness that we have had tremendous problems getting here. Well, we haven't gotten him here yet. As the previous filings would indicate, we have been trying over a year to find him. We have not had an opportunity to speak with him, and, therefore, there will be obvious difficulties and a lot of time that might be expended if the Prosecution is not able to put in its evidence, especially his testimony in the previous case, in written form. We have not had an opportunity to speak to him as yet; and as Your Honours are no doubt aware, the witness's evidence covers a huge amount of material. That's all I wish to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In light of the Defence submissions about the additional difficulties created by the Prosecution failure to relate the exhibits to the evidence of the witness, and in view of the potential importance of the evidence of the witness, we consider that it's appropriate - and this is a decision in principle - that his evidence should be given live. However, it will remain open to the Prosecution to suggest, in the course of his evidence, the admission of portions in writing, and we will review any such reasonable request made at the time. Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Given your decision, can you indicate to us when you would expect 98 bis submissions to commence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We will issue today, and at the latest tomorrow, decisions on all matters outstanding in relation to the admission of evidence. That means that if the witness is not produced on the 1st of May, the likelihood is that we will hear 98 bis submissions there and then. If the witness does give evidence, we will obviously give consideration to any motion you were to make in relation to the time at which your submissions should commence. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm wondering if we may consider your decision today that Mr. Lilic may testify beginning the 1st of May as in effect a final decision on that issue, or is it still open to the Prosecution to request additional delay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There will be written reasons given for this decision, and, therefore, I am reluctant to say more here. The only thing that is really preventing me being firmer about the implications of not producing the witness on the 1st of May is the potential accusation that the Trial Chamber has fettered its discretion in some way by making a decision that can't possibly take account of all the circumstances as at the 1st of May. But you can take it that the Bench is firmly of the view that we have already granted a great deal of indulgence to the Prosecution. I don't want to put it any higher than that at this stage. Your question is well intended, Mr. Ackerman, and you can see that we would hope next week not to be faced with a dilemma. Very well. We will adjourn now until -- can we check on the timing next week at 2:15?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The courtroom is currently assigned to us for 2.15 next Tuesday; but if 9.00 is available, then we will sit at 9.00. Inquiries will be made, and you will be notified about that. So far as 98 bis is concerned, it should be possible to sit for longer each day to get that dealt with, as long as courtroom space is available. But when it's a matter of evidence, it would only be with the agreement of the parties that we would extend evidence next week beyond the normal half day sitting. But if you wish us to do so, then at your request, we will do so, because it does provide a potential gain later in the preparation time for the Defence case. So we will adjourn now until 9.00 next Tuesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 1st day of May 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.13 p.m.,
